changelog.change: Added an extubation-window FiO2 note — avoid 100% washout (absorption atelectasis); ~70% is the practical target (Paschold, BJA 2026).

Initial entry — the daily readiness screen, SBT technique and pass/fail, SAT+SBT pairing, RSBI, cuff-leak test + prophylactic steroids, high-risk extubation to HFNC/NIV, the extubation procedure, post-extubation monitoring and reintubation, failure-to-wean work-up, and tracheostomy timing. Deepens the 'Weaning & extubation' section of ventilator-management.

summary: Screen every day, trial early, and separate the two questions: can they breathe (the SBT) and can they protect the airway (secretions, cough, cuff leak). Pass a 30-120 min SBT on low pressure support, extubate high-risk patients straight onto HFNC or NIV (never rescue NIV once failure is established), and watch the first 48-72 h. If a third SBT fails, stop guessing and hunt the reversible cause — cardiac, volume, neuromuscular, electrolyte, sedation, delirium.
whyThisMatters: Each extra ventilator day adds VAP, delirium, and ICU-acquired weakness risk, so an unweaned patient who could be liberated is being harmed by the delay — but a premature extubation that fails carries an independent mortality signal, and a *delayed* reintubation is worse still. The job is to extubate at the earliest moment the odds favour it, with the post-extubation support that matches the patient's risk already running, not to wait for certainty.
clinicalTakeaway: Run a daily readiness screen; when it passes, do a 30-120 minute SBT on pressure support 5-8 / PEEP 5 (or T-piece) paired with a sedation-interruption trial. Extubate if the SBT passes AND the patient follows commands, has a strong cough, and manageable secretions. For a high-risk patient (age > 65, COPD/CHF, > 7 days ventilated, prior failed SBT, weak cough) extubate directly onto HFNC — add NIV for hypercapnic COPD or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Do a cuff-leak test only in high-risk airways; a failed test means pretreat with methylprednisolone 20 mg IV q4h x 4 starting = 4 h before, not cancel. If NIV is needed for *established* post-extubation failure, reintubate instead. Three failed SBTs = look for weaning-induced pulmonary oedema, fluid overload, weakness, low phosphate/magnesium, oversedation, and delirium.

body.text: Assess every intubated patient at least once a day. All of the following should be true before an SBT:

items: The reason for intubation is resolving or resolved.
Oxygenation adequate: PaO2/FiO2 > 150-200, FiO2 = 0.4-0.5, PEEP = 5-8 cm H2O.
pH = 7.25 (compensated respiratory acidosis in a chronic CO2-retainer is acceptable at their baseline).
Haemodynamically stable: no or low-dose single vasopressor, no active myocardial ischaemia.
Able to initiate a spontaneous breath.
Mentation adequate for airway protection — follows simple commands, or a stable baseline deficit with a good cough and secretions that suction < every 1-2 h.
No planned return to theatre or procedure requiring deep sedation in the next 24 h.

body.text: Pair the screen with a Spontaneous Awakening Trial (sedation interruption) — coordinated SAT + SBT (ABC trial) shortens ventilation and ICU stay and lowers 1-year mortality versus usual sedation + SBT. Hold the SAT for active seizures, alcohol withdrawal, escalating pressors, active ischaemia, or paralysis.

items: Technique: pressure support 5-8 cm H2O with PEEP 5 (or CPAP 5, or a T-piece). The 2017 guideline suggests the *first* SBT be done with low pressure support rather than a T-piece, and last 30-120 minutes.

Duration: 30 minutes is enough for most; extend toward 120 minutes for high-risk or repeatedly failing patients (a 30-min PS trial and a 2-h T-piece trial give similar extubation success — JAMA 2019).

PASS if, for the whole trial: RR < 35 (ideally < 30), SpO2 = 90% (or PaO2 = 60 on FiO2 = 0.5), HR < 140 and no sustained change > 20%, SBP 90-180 with no new vasopressor need, and no distress — accessory muscle use, paradoxical abdominal motion, diaphoresis, agitation.
FAIL for any of the above, or an RSBI that climbs through the trial. A failed SBT → return to a comfortable rest mode (do NOT keep them working), find why (below), and re-screen in 24 h.

body.text: RSBI = respiratory rate / tidal volume in litres, measured on minimal/zero support after ~1 minute of spontaneous breathing. < 105 breaths/min/L predicts SBT success; = 105 predicts failure. Use it as an adjunct and a trend, not a gate — a borderline RSBI in an otherwise-ready patient should not stop an SBT, and a low RSBI does not override a clearly failing trial.

items: Cough strength: a weak cough (cannot clear secretions to the ETT, low peak cough flow) roughly triples extubation-failure risk independent of the SBT.
Secretion burden: frequent suctioning (< every 2 h) predicts failure.
Mental status: unable to follow commands adds risk but is not an absolute contraindication — in selected neuro patients with a good cough and airway reflexes, extubation still succeeds.

Cuff-leak test — only in patients at risk of post-extubation laryngeal oedema: traumatic or repeated intubation, intubation > 6 days, large ETT relative to airway, prior self-extubation with reintubation, airway burns/infection, or a previously failed cuff leak. Method: with the cuff deflated on volume-control, the expired tidal volume falls by < 110 mL (or < 10-15% of the delivered volume) = positive (concerning).

body.text: A positive cuff-leak test in a patient who is otherwise ready is a reason to PRETREAT, not to cancel. Give methylprednisolone 20 mg IV every 4 h for 4 doses (or 40 mg q4h), starting at least 4 h — ideally 12 h — before extubation, then re-check the leak. Have racemic epinephrine, steroids, heliox, and a reintubation/airway-exchange plan ready at the bedside for extubation.

items: Position sitting up (reverse Trendelenburg / 45° in obesity), suction the airway and mouth, pre-oxygenate, deflate the cuff and remove at end of a positive-pressure breath or during a cough.
Default post-extubation oxygen: conventional O2 for low-risk; step up as below for high-risk.

HIGH-RISK (extubate straight onto support): age > 65, chronic cardiac or respiratory disease, APACHE II > 12 on the extubation day, BMI > 30, = 1 failed SBT, mechanically ventilated > 7 days, = 2 comorbidities, weak cough or copious secretions.
High-risk without hypercapnia → high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) is at least as good as NIV for preventing reintubation and better tolerated.
High-risk WITH hypercapnic COPD, or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → prophylactic NIV (alternating with HFNC in the first 48 h in the highest-risk group lowers reintubation further).
Very high-risk / borderline airway → extubate over an airway-exchange catheter and keep it in situ during the observation window.

Do not wash out / extubate on 100% O2 by reflex — pure oxygen in poorly-ventilated alveoli causes absorption atelectasis (Paschold, BJA 2026: ~1067 mL end-expiratory lung-volume loss vs ~423 mL at lower FiO2). ~70% is the sweet spot: it matches 40% for atelectasis but gives the best post-extubation SpO2 stability. Keep 100% only if desaturation margin is genuinely the limiting concern.

body.text: Do NOT use NIV as rescue for ESTABLISHED post-extubation respiratory failure (rising work of breathing, hypercapnia, hypoxaemia already present) — it delays a needed reintubation and increases mortality. Prophylactic NIV started immediately at extubation in a high-risk patient is a different intervention with a different evidence base. Once failure is declared, reintubate.

items: Highest risk is the first 48-72 h. Watch: rising RR and work of breathing, stridor, agitation or somnolence, worsening gas exchange, and an escalating secretion/suction need.

Post-extubation stridor from laryngeal oedema → sit up, nebulised racemic epinephrine, IV dexamethasone or methylprednisolone, consider heliox as a bridge; low threshold to reintubate before it becomes a can't-ventilate airway.

Reintubation rate is ~10-15% and is independently associated with higher mortality — but the harm is worse when reintubation is DELAYED. If failure is established, reintubate promptly rather than escalating NIV/HFNC.
Reintubation is not the same as SBT failure: an SBT that fails means keep weaning; an extubation that fails means the airway or the pump could not sustain unassisted breathing outside the tube.

body.text: Simple weaning = extubated after the first SBT. Difficult = up to 3 SBTs or up to 7 days from the first SBT. Prolonged = > 3 SBTs or > 7 days. Once weaning is difficult, stop repeating identical trials and systematically look for reversible load/capacity mismatch:

rows: Weaning-induced pulmonary oedema — the switch to negative-pressure breathing raises LV preload and afterload. Suggested by a rising B-lines / E/e' / NT-proBNP or a haemoconcentration during the SBT. Diurese, optimise afterload/rate control, treat ischaemia; re-trial.
Cumulative positive fluid balance predicts weaning failure — target a neutral-to-negative balance once resuscitated.
Bronchospasm, secretions, auto-PEEP, pleural effusion (drain a large one), abdominal distension, chest-wall oedema.

ICU-acquired weakness, critical-illness polyneuropathy/myopathy, phrenic nerve injury (post-cardiac-surgery, central-line), residual neuromuscular blockade, Guillain-Barré / myasthenia. Early mobilisation and PT; minimise steroids + paralytics together.
Replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium, calcium; avoid overfeeding (high CO2 load) and metabolic alkalosis (blunts respiratory drive).
Accumulated sedatives (especially benzodiazepines), opioid load, delirium, and untreated pain or anxiety. Switch to light/analgesia-first sedation, treat delirium, mobilise.
Hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, anaemia limiting O2 delivery, malnutrition.

items: For prolonged weaning, use a protocolised gradual reduction of pressure support (or progressively longer T-piece periods) with full rest overnight, plus daily SBT screening.

Tracheostomy: TracMan showed no survival benefit to early (< 10 days) versus late placement — decide by day 7-10 on the trajectory (airway protection needs, expected further weeks of support, secretion clearance, patient comfort and communication), not a fixed day.
